preamble: The voiced alveolar stop /d/ is realized as the alveolar flap [ɾ] between vowels. In North American, Australian and New Zealand English /d/ flaps before an unstressed vowel just as /t/ does, so that ladder and latter become homophonous or nearly so; in Tagalog [ɾ] was traditionally the intervocalic allophone of /d/, which still shows in derived forms such as dami 'quantity' → marami 'many'.

examples.note: Homophonous or nearly so with latter in North American English.
Flapping applies before syllabic /l/ as well as before unstressed vowels.
Prefix ma- puts root-initial /d/ between vowels, where it surfaces as [ɾ]; /ɾ/ was traditionally an allophone of /d/.

context: Between vowels (in English, before an unstressed vowel or syllabic /l/)
allophones_note: In English the underlying /d/ surfaces as [ɾ] intervocalically, neutralizing the /t/–/d/ contrast at the surface; in Tagalog [ɾ] and [d] were once allophones and the alternation survives in prefixed forms.
sources: Wells, J. C. (1982). Accents of English. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511611759
